This was a thing of fifty years ago.

In the spring of 1931 the Commandant, Mr. Chiang, at his official residence at the Xianglin Temple in Nanjing, received us in batches—more than a hundred academy classmates newly returned from posts all over the country—for a word apart with each.

Since I had passed through enlisted training and graduated and been assigned out, apart from the mass exhortations and the roll-calls in ranks, this was the first time the Commandant had spoken with me face to face and alone in his office. On that occasion it was Zeng Kuoqing, of the first class, who made the introduction.

The Commandant wore a Zhongshan tunic and sat serenely in the chair behind his desk, on which lay a roster copied out on ten-column paper; in his hand he held a thick two-colored pencil, red and blue. As I marched up to the desk and came to a halt, bowed, and raised my eyes to look at him, what struck me most deeply was that the Commandant's eyes were bright and piercing, his bearing awe-inspiring and stern, so that one dared not look him full in the face.

The Commandant first asked after such family matters as my native province and county, whether my parents were living or dead, how many brothers I had; asking and listening as he went, and checking the roster against my answers. Then he asked what work interested me, and I answered boldly and from the heart: "The military work of the troops has grown strange to me now; work of any other kind I should be glad to learn." I thought these words would anger him, but I saw the Commandant make a mark on the roster, with no sign of displeasure.

This audience lasted, from first to last, about three minutes, and he put no more than three or four questions to me; the process being so simple, I felt nothing special at the time. Thinking it over afterward, I guessed that the Commandant was perhaps looking me over and hearing me out, making a selection through observation; as to his standard, that only the old gentleman himself would know.
Three or four days later word came that, out of more than a hundred of us, fourteen had been marked out to open a class and undergo training. On the list my name stood last.

This small training unit was named the "Central Military Academy Special Research Class," with Feng Ti, director of the academy's political department, serving concurrently as its director, and Shen Zunhui as its secretary. Zhang Zhizhong, then the education chief of the Central Military Academy, seemed to take no part in the matter.

This training class was styled "Special," and in fact it truly was different from the ordinary run of training bodies. First, it had no premises of its own: making do as best we could, we set a few single-drawer long tables in one office of the academy's political department, two men to a wooden bench, and so contrived. Second, no uniform was prescribed; a Zhongshan tunic or a Western suit would do, so long as one did not wear a long gown and short jacket. Because we wore no uniform, there was no military discipline either. Besides this, there was no fixed timetable of work and rest, no need to come and go by the clock; coming late or leaving early was never interfered with, so that one may say the academy authorities granted us a high degree of self-government—and just because of that, we too knew well enough to conduct ourselves with self-respect. As for the courses, apart from specially engaged lectures, there was ordinarily no instructor to teach us.

The courses we studied were several books the Commandant himself had prescribed, such as the *Complete Works of Lu Xiangshan*, the *Complete Works of Wang Yangming*, the *Complete Works of Zeng Wenzheng*, Qi Jiguang's *Records on the Governance of Troops*, and *The Theoretical System of the Three Principles of the People*. After reading them on our own, we had to write up what we had gained into notes; these, once gathered, were submitted once a week to the Commandant for his review, and came back marked, often with comments in the margins.
Of these vast and profound works of Confucian learning, not even a third of us fourteen could truly read them "through," and I was one of the rest.

During the training there was, however, one thing laid down as a hard rule: that, except on Sundays, we must at noon gather for a common meal in the academy's "Gong-Character Mess Hall." The Gong-Character Mess Hall was in those days a new-style building that could hold several hundred; its arrangement was neat, its cleaning spotless, the rows of dining tables making a straight line whether you looked across them or along them, each in its proper place. The tables were spread with white cloth, and the tableware too was uniformly white porcelain; if one were to find fault, perhaps the one thing wanting was a vase of bright fresh flowers. Because the building was shaped like the character *gong* (工), it was called the Gong-Character Mess Hall.

The Commandant would arrive at about five minutes past twelve; first the duty officer would call the commands—all rise, be seated—and the crowd would answer, "Begin," and then all fell to together. Though every man was careful to make no sound, there was still, now and then, the unavoidable clink of tableware knocking together.

The eating took about ten minutes; one by one everyone laid down his bowl and chopsticks and tidied things up, sat straight in his place, drew up his chest, and listened respectfully to the Commandant's exhortation on matters of the spirit.

Before the Commandant stood a seating chart bearing our names, and whenever he had finished speaking he would now and then call on someone by name to answer a question. Those who could speak freely and reply without a stumble were not often seen. Everyone carried an anxious heart, dreading to be called on and made a fool of on the spot; yet there were also those itching to try.

In the second month after the class opened, at the instance of the senior elder brothers, we fourteen put our names to a report requesting the Commandant to permit the restoration of our party membership and academy enrollment—for at that time all fourteen of us had, each for a different reason, had our party membership and academy enrollment struck off. The Commandant wrote his ruling in brush: "The restoration of party membership and academy enrollment is permitted," and signed it "Zhongzheng." The date was around June 1931. The original was at first kept by Han Jun (Zhongjin) of the first class. Before long the Central Military Academy Special Party Branch issued a party card of the "junyu" series; and separately, senior brother Tian Zailong, in charge of the "Investigation Section for Military Academy Graduates," notified us that the restoration would be "annotated" in the graduate registers of our several classes.

Of this ruling of the Commandant's, all fourteen of us kept a photographic copy. The one I held has, over these several decades of running about north and south, east and west, ended up I know not where. Thinking it over carefully, I believe that, for reasons of secrecy, it was most likely destroyed by my own hand.

Of us fourteen I was the youngest in years and the lowest in class; among us were seven senior elder brothers of the first class—Han Jun, Chen Lie, Huang Yong, Yu Yong, Wu Naixian, Xu Huizhi, and Liu Jiwen; two of the second class, Zhang Yanyuan and Cao Xu; none of the third class; one only of the fourth, Zheng Sikang; and four in all of the fifth class, namely Han Jiwen, Xia Dakang, Xie Juecheng, and the present writer.

The monthly living allowance the fourteen of us drew was not the same, but was granted according to class in descending order: the first class eighty yuan, the second seventy, and so on down to the fifth at only forty. In truth, forty yuan in those days, for a single man with no family to carry, ought to have been quite enough.

Those with families all lived outside; we few bachelors lived in the academy staff dormitory, two men assigned to a room, and I roomed with Xie Juecheng. Xie was gifted at song and recitation and steeped in an especially strong literary temper; he would not read the prescribed books, but lay all day over his desk writing new-style verse, and when the mood took him would declaim a few lines aloud—so that at the time he was reckoned an odd fellow.

By the fourth month of training, two of our classmates suddenly vanished; at first we supposed they had taken personal leave and would be back in a few days, but, as it turned out, two whole months passed, we all graduated and left, and we never saw them again.—Both were Cantonese: one was Wu Naixian, the first-class elder brother; the other was Han Jiwen, a fifth-class classmate, also called Shangying, who had shared a table with me during the training.

At the time no one paid the matter any special heed, nor did the classmates discuss it. Only years afterward did we learn that they had gone to Shanghai and carried through a great and secret affair. Since it is called "secret," then, though the years are long gone by and things have changed, it is still best to "keep it." Yet this much may be said: the affair was one of grave moment, and it holds a page too in the history of political-party activity; only it is a pity that the few who knew the most of it have all passed away.
To speak now of what befell the twelve of us:

When the six-month training was up, just after the September 18th Incident, the Commandant, Mr. Chiang, by his own hand directed that the twelve of us report to the Party Central. Having reported, we waited a long while, but nothing came of it, and not one of us was assigned any work. For what reason, I do not know to this day. Having no other choice, we could only part there and each go his own way.

I had no social connections to speak of, and just as I was at a stand, neither able to advance nor to retreat, the two senior elder brothers Huang Yong (Jianqiu) and Zhang Yanyuan (Binghua) took kind pity on me and had me move in with them. Neither had brought family; they had sublet a room on an upper floor of a house in Zhongyi Lane in Huapailou, already furnished. At the time the two elder brothers slept in a great iron bed hung with a mosquito-net, while I, alone, laid a pallet on the floor at night and rolled up the bedding again in the morning.

The three of us were seldom together; but sometimes we would buy a little fish and meat, cook it over the pump-stove, and the three of us fall to at the table with a will—and sweet it was. In after years, whenever we met and spoke of those days, the taste of it was with us still.

One afternoon a guest came calling. He first shook hands and exchanged greetings with Jianqiu and Binghua, and then, with a smile, held out to me too the hand of friendship. Brother Jianqiu made haste to introduce us to each other, saying: "This little brother is Chen Gongshu, of the fifth class; this elder brother is Dai Li, Dai Yunong, of the sixth class." That the fifth class should be called "little brother" and the sixth "elder brother"—there was something odd in this form of introduction.

To look at, he was a good deal older than I: heavy brows and large eyes, a high-bridged nose and prominent cheekbones; though not tall, he seemed very solid and firmly built, a man one might call uncommon in feature and extraordinary in bearing. This first impression was a strong one; as to what he made of me, that there was no telling.

Once classmates are gathered together, they fall to talking without ceremony. Though all four of us spoke ordinary Mandarin, brother Huang Jianqiu was from Pingjiang in Hunan, brother Zhang Binghua from Meixian in Guangdong; and the guest, Dai Yunong, from Jiangshan in Zhejiang—the local burrs in our speech were all rather thick, yet the talk went so well that, had the light not dimmed, we should not have felt that the sun was already sinking in the west.

Brother Jianqiu proposed that we all go out for a bite. Not far beyond Zhongyi Lane there was a small local eating-house, by the name of the Yingfeng Tavern, modest in its scale, only a single storey over a ground floor. We ordered a few dishes and called for a pot of wine, and the whole came to less than two yuan; everyone thought it not bad at all.

From then on Dai Yunong often dropped in to sit with us, and now and then we would go together to see a film. One day, as we were playing mahjong with the landlady, Dai Yunong came again; seeing that I was losing, he made a great show of coming to my aid like a knight drawing his sword, bade me stand up, and played a few hands in my stead—but from the way he drew and discarded tiles, he seemed no old hand at the game.

I once asked brothers Jianqiu and Binghua what work this classmate Dai did. They told me they knew only that he was at the Commandant's residence, but were not clear what post he held. I pressed on, puzzled: if he served at the residence, why, when the Commandant had just now stepped down and returned to Fenghua, had he not gone along? The two elder brothers gave me no straight answer, only mumbled a vague "hm" and let it go.

As we came to know one another better, and our acquaintance deepened not a little, Dai Yunong once asked me out of the blue: "Brother Gongshu, do you know a man named Cao Xiaoqing?" I answered: "Know him! We did our enlisted training in the same company, were in the same platoon and the same squad, and slept the one over the other in a double bunk. He is a graduate of Meiji University in Japan, and I got no further than middle school, yet the two of us actually became fast friends; he could not even wind his puttees properly, and I used to tease him for it."

I paused a moment and then added: "Since he went up into the political science course of this academy with the fourth class, and I, falling behind through illness, was put into the infantry course of the fifth—we parted, and from then till now I have never seen him again."

Dai Yunong said, in dead earnest: "And if Cao Xiaoqing were in Nanjing at this moment?" I said, "Then I should go and see him at once." And then I asked back: "Has he really come to Nanjing?" Dai Yunong shook his head and said, "I only hope he might come to Nanjing."

That Dai Yunong should ask this quite bewildered me; only later did he tell me that Cao Xiaoqing was then in Shanghai, attached to Hu Hanmin and working up a "New Kuomintang," engaged in splittist activity against the government.
Later still I came to see that Dai Yunong's sudden mention of Cao Xiaoqing had in it something of a sounding-out, or a test.
Before long the Commandant returned to the capital to take up his heavy charge, and the times Dai Yunong met with us grew fewer, and each visit shorter.

Brother Jianqiu and I went on as before, but Zhang Binghua showed himself uncommonly busy, sometimes not coming home the whole night, and even when he did come back to rest, his rest was cut short, and in a turn he was off again. I guessed that brother Binghua was very likely taking part in some important and secret work.
This was just the time of the "January 28th," when the Japanese invaders pushed into Shanghai and our army fought back with valor.

Of late, whenever Dai Yunong met with us, he would remark: "If you have a report to submit to the Commandant, you can hand it to me to pass up—it is the handier way." Each time I answered: "I have no request to make, nor any memorial to offer; I dare not trouble the Commandant." Saying so, I felt myself very much in the right. In truth I was too thick-witted: the "report" he meant was not so narrow a thing as I imagined, and it is a pity that at the time I could not take his meaning.
When the "January 28th" affair drew to a close, the National Government moved to Luoyang, the Commandant, Mr. Chiang, took up quarters at Xuzhou, and Dai Yunong stayed on in Nanjing.

One day Dai Yunong came looking for me, a heavy, bulging large envelope in his hand, sealed with wax on the back. He said he was "entrusting" me to make a special trip to Xuzhou without delay and deliver it in person to the aide-de-camp, Dai Songyi.

Hearing that the Commandant was then quartered at Xuzhou, and that Dai Yunong wanted me to go there and charged me to deliver it in person to the aide Dai—its importance may be imagined. Without a second thought I agreed. He gave me two travel warrants and a little for the road, and before I set out told me further: "There is a special train standing at Xuzhou station, with armed guards near it, and plainclothes guards too—you are sure to spot them, I think; ask anyone, and you will find this aide Dai. Once the letter is delivered, just have him sign for it."

That very night I reached Xuzhou, and before I had even left the platform I found the aide Dai Songyi; I handed the wax-sealed envelope to him in person, and he turned it over and over, took out a name card and wrote a few words on it by way of a receipt, gave no instructions by word of mouth, and simply sent me back.
Looking at the card, I learned that his rank was lieutenant colonel and that he was from Yunnan; on inquiring later, I found he too was an academy classmate.

Back in Nanjing, I went for the first time to the Dai residence at No. 53 Ji'e Lane. It was a not-very-tidy one-storey house; once inside the door, one turned crookedly this way and that through several bends before reaching the parlor. In a well-appointed household the floor would be spread with carpet; his was spread with straw matting. Because the ground was damp and there was no help for it, he made shift in poverty.

I gave Dai Yunong the card that served as a receipt, and so completed his "commission." Seeing that he was busy, I was about to take my leave when he suddenly asked me: "Have you any close friend among the classmates from Fujian province?" I thought a moment and hit on Lian Mou, a fourth-class classmate and a good friend, also known as Lian Liangshun. I answered that there was such a man, first-rate in both ability and appearance; but I did not know what he wanted a Fujian man for. Dai Yunong gave no straight answer, only asked that I introduce them with all speed.
I introduced them, and they met.
Dai Yunong sent Lian Mou to Fuzhou to set up a working station—of which at the time I knew nothing, nor had brother Liangshun bidden me farewell before he left.
Judging from these two matters, where lay Dai Yunong's mission? One might guess well over half of it.

In March I moved from Zhongyi Lane to Mingwalang, living alone in a small inn. Brother Binghua had already been sent to Guangdong—or, by another account, to Hong Kong—and with him went Wu Jinfu (Naixian). When we parted, though we did not say aloud what we were going to do, we already understood each other in our hearts.

Brother Jianqiu, too, brought his good lady over and rented another house. He had made it clear to me that he did not mean to join the work Dai Yunong led, but would rather stand in a helping place; and so indeed it proved.

Mingwalang is very near Sandaogaojing, and the Military Academy Alumni Association stood on that very street of Sandaogaojing. With this for a hub, in the small inns of the surrounding quarter lodged a good many academy classmates—some waiting for work, some seeing to their registration—all mixed together in a great bustle. My own moving to Mingwalang was neither to seek work nor to register, but entirely at Dai Yunong's wish: he wanted me to keep a closer eye on the classmates' doings, and above all on any activity out of the ordinary run, beyond the bounds. Seen simply, it was a small matter he had entrusted to me; put another way, it was as good as assigning me a mission. I did not quite grasp it—this was what is called "intelligence work." But the one thing I remember most clearly is that he never paid me any wage. That is to say, I was still in the walk-on stage.

By the general record, at the end of February 1931 Dai Yunong had already been marked out as head of the "Special Services Department." This "Special Services Department" was no organ of government, but came under the newly formed secret revolutionary organization, the "Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People." After a period of preparation, it was formally established in Nanjing on the first of April; and so the "Juntong" afterward set "April First" as its founding anniversary.

Dai Yunong perished in an air crash on 17 March 1946; and so the "April First commemoration" was moved and merged into "March 17th," known in short as the "March 17th Commemorative Assembly." Ever after, the "March 17th Assembly" was held year by year, and after the move to Taiwan it went on without a break; while the late President lived, he came in person to speak each year. It is indeed a day worth commemorating.
Looking back, in that season of our first acquaintance Dai Yunong already bore a mission of "liaison."

Whether there was at that time a unit called the "Liaison Group," I cannot say. Only in the *Chronicle of Mr. Dai Yunong* is it recorded: "In December 1931, in order to bring about unity and meet the national peril together, Mr. Chiang resigned his post as chairman of the National Government and other offices and left the capital for his native place. Before setting out he ordered Mr. Dai Li to take charge of liaison, the chief task being to unite the revolutionary forces centered on the Whampoa students, to reconnoiter the enemy's movements, and to suppress the reactionaries. Thereupon organizations were set up and active work carried on in Nanjing, Shanghai, Hangzhou, Beiping, Tianjin, Hankou, Hong Kong, Guangzhou, Jiangxi, and other places."

From this one may see clearly that Dai Yunong then bore a mission of "liaison"; that is beyond doubt. But the so-called "Liaison Group" was probably no formal establishment, only a name used for the time being to stand for this line of work.

As for the statement that, in December 1931, organizations were already "set up and active work carried on in Nanjing, Shanghai, Hangzhou, Beiping, Tianjin, Hankou, Hong Kong, Guangzhou, Jiangxi, and other places"—this too is not wholly so. Of other places I dare not speak; but I was myself the one who founded the work in Beiping, and I was not sent to Beiping until November 1932.
This is one proof of how very hard a thing it is to compose writings of a historical kind.

Of Dai Yunong's "Special Services Department" there are many tales; for his class-standing and position among the senior cadres of the "Lixingshe" were both below those of others, so how did this heavy charge come to be laid on him? By Dai Yunong's own account:

"At eight in the evening on 26 February 1932, in the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum park at Nanjing, I received from the Leader the order to establish the Special Services Department. The Leader supported me, and I of course bore absolute responsibility; but on the morning of the next day a certain comrade—now gone abroad, whose name I had better not speak—came to pull me down. He said, 'As for the personnel and funds of the Special Services Department, the Commandant has told him to take charge of them.' The next day I reported to the Leader and asked to resign; in the end it was not allowed, and a full year later the Leader told me that there were still people coming to attack me. …"

From this passage one may know that his taking up the "Special Services Department" was entirely by the support and favor of the Commandant, Mr. Chiang. And that was because he had long before a record of distinguished work behind him.

Setting aside the deeds already told in the *Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong*, the *Chronicle of Mr. Dai Yunong*, the *Life of Dai Li*, and other writings—which I shall not repeat—I heard from an old man more than ten years my senior, who would not let me give his name, much about Mr. Dai Yunong's conduct; and since this is hearsay, I set it down for what it is worth, as anecdotes of Mr. Dai's unrecorded history—or perhaps as some corroboration of his earlier working career.

Early on, between 1928 and 1930, Mr. Dai Yunong, Mr. Tian Zailong, Mr. Wang Tianmu, Mr. Hu Baoyi, and others had organized in Kaifeng, Henan, a "Three People's Principles Great Chivalry Corps," which on the one hand made contact with and drew in patriots of high resolve, and on the other could serve as a feeler for intelligence.

Again, one year, the black-hearted Feng Yuxiang hired with money a band of desperadoes—Middle Easterners who called themselves Syrians—and slipped them into Nanjing meaning to commit an assassination; Dai Yunong got word of it beforehand and so cracked the case.

Again, in Shanghai, a set of secret-society men, meaning to pick a quarrel on some pretext, put terms to the authorities and talked loudly of "the cut," failing which they would do thus and so; and it was Dai Yunong and his men who came forward and smoothed it over.

Mr. Dai Yunong never made a show of himself; of such matters as those set out above there must be many more, and I never once heard him bring them up. What I know, or rather what I understand, is that Dai Yunong's combative spirit was strong: he meant to overcome every adversity; yet he was not stubborn, and while holding fast to principle he had a superhuman knack of adapting to any circumstance. As for his knowing men and using them well, that is known to all who know anything; and, more than the common run can reach, many a hard "iron man" of fleeting fame, once under his hand, would turn soft enough to wind round a finger.

I was in the little inn at Mingwalang, sitting stuffily over my writing alone, when a man I had never met, who gave his surname as Pan, came to talk with me—what an abrupt thing that was. Without asking my leave, he struck up a conversation, ranging from my family circumstances to my ideological schooling, and from the state of the nation to the international situation; and he said, in fact, more than I answered. Turn it over as I might, I truly could not make out what he was driving at.
As this uninvited guest was leaving, he left me word that in a few days someone else would come to talk with me again.

After he had gone, the more I thought the worse it sat with me: since I did not understand where he came from, why had I answered his questions so readily and without demur? Was it that I had already been cowed by that irresistible force of his coming? Or had I sensed all along that he was one of our own, come by order?

Two days later, sure enough, someone came again to talk with me—this time it was fellow student Yi, of my own class, whom I had met before but had little to do with. He beat about the bush no longer, but said outright: "Now a political organization full of new life has been born, one may say a product of a great age: whole-heartedly upholding our Commandant as Leader, with the academy classmates for its backbone, practicing vigorously the Three Principles of the People, reviving the revolutionary spirit, restoring Chinese culture, sacrificing personal interest, with an iron will and strict discipline, obeying the organization's decisions, and, under the Commandant's brilliant leadership, opening up a new order together."

He asked me: "Would you be willing to join such an organization?" The words in my heart were: "I had meant all along to gather comrades and get up just such an organization; but I am of small account and my word carries no weight—I am simply not qualified, and besides I should not dare to propose it openly." As I was thinking so, he pressed me again: "Have you any further considerations?" And so I put my own question back to him: "That comrade Pan who talked with me a few days ago—was he sent by this organization?" Fellow student Yi told me: "Yes; this is one of the procedures by which the organization takes in comrades, and may be explained as a necessary step. But a visit so sudden as that easily leaves the other party at a loss, and may even bring on needless misunderstanding; it seems it ought to be improved."

At the last I asked him naively: "Why was I singled out?" He answered with a smile: "Someone recommended you, I suppose." I asked again: "Can you tell me who?" But he only smiled and did not answer, and before he left he hinted that I had passed this barrier too.

Whether I filled out many kinds of forms and went through what procedures, or whether the record of their talks with me took the place of those procedures, I can no longer remember. Within a few days word came, and I knew I had indeed been "taken in" as a comrade of the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association." At the time, in my feeling, to be able to become a member of a secret revolutionary organization could not but bring a certain pride of mind, for I was now a mainstay in the revolutionary camp.

At that time, and even for some while after, I had no notion at all that above the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association" there was a core organization—the "Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People"; I understood only that, besides the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association" (the "Military Association" for short), there was a sister organization parallel to it, the "Revolutionary Youth Comrades Association" (the "Youth Association" for short). In plain terms, I had been "taken in" only at the second tier, still on the "periphery" of the core.

Not long after I joined—some three or five days, I dare say—Dai Yunong "called me up" to undergo secret-service training, so that I never did take part in the organizational activity of the "Military Association"—such as its small-group meetings.

Most puzzling of all was that the secret-service training ran a full six months, and yet the "Military Association" never once made contact with me. I did not understand: could it be that this "training class" had no connection at all with that "revolutionary body"? By rights, though their natures differed, there should surely have been some link. Who would have guessed there was a deep mystery in it—a point I shall account for later in the course of events.

In 1979 I read in a magazine this passage: "Among the various training bodies run by the Lixingshe was an 'Intelligence Personnel Training Class,' with Dai Li as director, established at the end of March 1932; the trainees were all selected by examination from graduates of the various classes of the Military Academy, and from persons of every walk with an aptitude for intelligence. To meet the Lixingshe's needs, it gathered and drew on choice teaching materials, instructors, and cadre officers from China, Japan, Germany, Russia, Britain, and America, and gave a strict, secret, short-term training in intelligence business."

This piece, written by a senior cadre of the "Lixingshe," proves one point: that between the "Lixingshe," its peripheral organization the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association," and the "secret-service training body" there was a definite relation of subordination, of master and man. Or, one may say, that this "training class" was run by the "Lixingshe."

But the several points about the intelligence training class raised in that piece still differ greatly from the actual state of things as I lived them. This is hard to say, for even a hair's difference of standpoint can breed a great divergence. Where they differ, I shall set out below, point by point.

At that time, in 1932, though I was a comrade of the "Military Association," what I knew was no more than this much. Beyond it, half was rumor and half surmise, and none of that can count. The greatest surprise of all was that I never dreamed Dai Yunong held so high a position in this organization.
The long passage below sets down in detail how I answered the call-up and underwent the training:

In May 1932 Dai Yunong sought me out; without first asking my consent, he seemed already certain that I could not but agree to his request. Neither explaining nor accounting for it, he asked me to seek out, among the academy classmates of the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh classes, thirty men to undergo a special training of no very long term. Besides this, the note of caution he gave me was: better, within a week, to furnish him a list with brief personal particulars attached, for his use.

In only three days, in the small inns around the "Investigation Section for Military Academy Graduates" at Sandaogaojing and Mingwalang, I gained the consent of thirty classmates. Some got to the bottom of it; some did not care to look far into it; some were half in doubt, for they could not fathom that I should have this sort of connection, or rather did not wholly believe there was any such thing in it. Yet most felt this was a rather novel affair.
Mr. Dai Yunong took the whole list, without a moment's thought. The total was thirty men, myself included.

The address of the training class was in the rear court of the Investigation Section for Military Academy Graduates at Sandaogaojing, one entering and leaving always by the main gate of Sandaogaojing. This site was not large in area, with some old-style buildings of no set plan. A rough, uneven courtyard was opened up for a drill ground. In one side wall facing south a small narrow door had newly been cut. Call it a door—it was really more like a hole, admitting only a short man, bent low, one at a time. Beyond the narrow door was a little alley only a few feet wide, down which not even a man-pulled cart could pass.
On the far side of that little alley rose another high wall, and within that wall was the "Honggongci." Later, the "Honggongci Training Class" of the Juntong's records took its rise from this.

The formal, full title of the training class was the "Special Service Police Training Class of the General Staff Headquarters." Its director was held concurrently by Shen Tingchan, then chief of the Second Bureau of the General Staff Headquarters; its deputy director by Wang Gupan, chief of the Capital Police Department. Plainly the director and deputy director alike held their posts in name only, and in fact seldom showed their faces. At the opening, at graduation, or when the Leader came, they would put in an appearance, and answer the roll, and that was all.

Under the class headquarters it was divided into sections or subjects, each going its own way; three sections, as I recall. Mr. Zheng Jiemin was in charge of instruction; Mr. Dai Yunong presided over the class's affairs under the title of "administration"; Mr. Li Shizhen was in charge of moral discipline and served concurrently as team leader.

This was the early form of secret-service training in our country; being newly begun, it had only the rough shape of a thing. Yet, high and low, inside and out, the whole class was charged with an air of mystery.

I really could not understand it: since this training class was in fact Mr. Dai Yunong's responsibility, why did he go under a title of "administration"? Was it that his standing was not weighty enough? That his academy class was too low? Or for fear of exposing his identity? There must surely have been some reason in it.

There was another thing past understanding, and it was this: since the "Special Service Police Training Class" was run by the "Lixingshe," yet from the opening to the graduation, over half a year, the Commandant came in person many times—while not one of the senior cadres of the "Lixingshe" was ever seen to come. What was this for? It is truly a thing to ponder. These matters of personnel were too tangled; I was not yet up to analyzing them.

As for the training class's furnishings, to call them merely "crude" hardly seems enough; add "shabby," and it comes near the mark. In saying so I mean no mockery, but only to show how hard the founding was—truly a road of thorns and brambles.

The class headquarters office was set in two low rooms, and the several office desks of unequal height were each spread with a piece of blue cloth. The blue cloth was new, and though it covered the mottled desktops, it could not hide the worn desk legs. On the desks lay a few articles of stationery, and besides them a jangling call-bell.
The rooms had no doors left; over each doorway hung a white curtain, which the wind, blowing, kept endlessly astir.

The row of rooms diagonally across from the office was the trainees' dormitory. Dim it was, and moreover had doors but no windows. The air within did not circulate well; add the damp of the mildew season, and there was a foul reek fit to sting the nose. The beds were in upper and lower bunks, boarded together of thin planks, and creaked the moment one lay down; even to turn over was to rouse all the neighbors. Bedding and sheets were one's own, of five hues and every sort; and if strict tidiness of quarters were demanded, that would be hard.

The classroom for lessons was the great assembly hall, and all our gatherings were held there too. The platform was built of planks, standing a foot or more off the ground. On it was an oiled, glossy black table, reckoned the most eye-catching new object of all. Behind it was mounted an old blackboard; call it black—it was really dark gray, and would fade paler still in time. The platform was small in area, holding at most a dozen men standing; set out chairs and sit down, and it held only six or seven. To the left and right of the platform was a small plank-built side room each, used to store books, lecture notes, and materials for experiments, and to serve too as a place for the instructors to rest a little.

In the classroom fifteen long tables were set out in neat order, ranged in three rows, two men to a long bench, holding just thirty. The classroom, hall, and gathering-place—an all-purpose great room—was bare of any adornment; only in the first few days of the term were some gaudy slogans pasted on the surrounding walls. The wording of the slogans held nothing striking; as for that couplet later composed in Mr. Dai Yunong's own hand—"the eyes and ears of the Leader; hands and feet to the brethren"—it was not yet there at this time.

The mess was but a wall away from the classroom, seven or eight square tables with long benches set round them. Of the three daily meals, by rule it was steamed bread and rice gruel in the morning, and rice at noon and evening. Six to a table was the rule, with four dishes and a soup served; teaching staff and trainees ate all together, the fare exactly the same. As for whether the food was good or bad—it filled the belly, that was all; but no one ever complained of it.

Washing and bathing were set in an inconspicuous corner beside the mess. In the open, with no cover at all, a few planks front and back served for a screen. With an enamel basin and a great wooden tub, one could draw water at will and rinse off. The murmur of the drain running off—was that not a sight in itself?
The hardest days to bear were the sweltering ones of summer, past enduring; and pray for a fall of rain, and then the roof would leak.

The team leader, Mr. Li Shizhen, enforced a strict military discipline. Not only did he take charge, he gave himself heart and soul to it, throwing himself into his duty around the clock, twenty-four hours a day, well-nigh without sleep or rest.

During the training all Sundays were canceled outright; not only were we not allowed out, we could not so much as make a telephone call to the outside. In other words, we were cut off from every tie with the outer world. And so, in those six months, except when we came and went in ranks for course practice, we never once, any one of us alone, walked out through that hole-like narrow door.

At the two musters, morning and evening, team leader Li Shizhen took the roll in person, six months on end without a day's slackening, and never careless by so much as one "check." Above all, that dose of exhortation after the evening roll was both tedious and long, and truly wearisome past bearing.

At our lessons, team leader Li came into the classroom along with us at almost every session, and did not leave until the instructor had begun to speak; yet in the twinkling of an eye one would find him standing there again. The classmates rather grudged him his fussiness, but on the whole respected him, and in fact he was indeed a good team leader.

Mr. Li Shizhen was also an academy classmate, and had studied "higher police" in Japan; in the class he too took charge of one course, called simply "Higher Police," and seemed the type of no great natural gifts who yet strives hard to get ahead.

Mr. Li Shizhen and I, after parting then, have never met again in the more than forty years since. It is said Mr. Li made quite a name in police affairs; and there is a rumor that at one time he even contended with Mr. Dai Yunong for control of the police—I do not know whether it is so. And if it were, I think that "age" is long since past.
The date of the opening, according to the *Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong*, was June 1932; by my own memory it was May—perhaps I misremember.

The opening ceremony had a simple, solemn rite; the chairman of the Military Affairs Commission and commandant of the Military Academy, our Leader, Mr. Chiang, came in person to administer the oath. He who attended the Leader as he stepped into the hall was neither the class director, Shen Tingchan, nor the deputy director, Wang Gupan, still less any secretary or standing cadre of the "Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People," but Dai Li, head of the administration section of the training class.
Into the hall came only the Leader and Dai Li; all the others, some in military uniform and some in plain clothes, halted outside the door—a somewhat uncommon scene, this.

Beforehand, each trainee had a mimeographed copy of the oath; the Leader raised his left hand and led the reading, and Dai Li and the trainees read it after him once more; the reading done, Dai Li at once gathered up all the oaths and burnt them then and there. The whole hall was solemn and silent.
The Leader gave his exhortation, urging us to be able to sacrifice the lesser self, to guard the nation, and to be a nameless hero.

The oath taken, we began our lessons in earnest. As to the courses, Mr. Zheng Jiemin, in charge of instruction, was indeed at great pains; his greatest difficulty was the finding of teachers. For a training of this kind, being the first of its sort with no precedent, what subjects were to be set out? What teaching materials were needed? Where were instructors to be respectfully engaged, and who was equal to it? For a time no satisfying answer could be had to any of it, and, feeling their way forward apart, no one could produce a good plan.

As for what a certain magazine said—"it gathered and drew on choice teaching materials and instructors from China, Japan, Germany, Russia, Britain, and America, and gave a training in intelligence business"—those are fine words, and no more.

In fact, in whatever age, down to the world of today, materials of this kind are for the most part compiled by each country for itself. Think of it: what country would honestly hand this whole set of things over to be taught to foreigners? Would that not be truly to give a man a handle against oneself? One can only say that the foreign goods we had translated could, at the very most, be ranked as "reference material."
Now see the course of study we received:

The most basic was still the political course, which took in party doctrine, political theory, international questions, and the like. To my own mind, this course ought to have been presided over by the senior cadres of the "Lixingshe"; but they did not come either. Why this should be so is past understanding.
Shorthand—the "Zhang Cai shorthand system" was chosen, taught by an heir of Zhang Cai's line; well taught, and hardest to learn.

Quick sketching—those who came to teach were the Liang brothers. I recall that Mr. Liang Dingming once took us to his "XiangguSi studio" to view his great oil paintings. The unfinished picture seemed to be "The Battle of Mianhu."
Photography—this took in the use of the camera and development in the darkroom, and the teacher was likewise a master, though which one I cannot recall.

Driving—divided into motorcar and motorcycle driving, both practiced; but, hampered by time, most of us, save a few, never learned it, and the instructor was Zhou Qibang, an elder brother of the first class.

Demolition—we all had some grounding, so this time it was as good as revision, with more variety besides; what everyone enjoyed most was making our own blasting cans. A bang, and how happy we were—great fun, too.

Shooting—this took in the stripping and assembling of firearms of every kind. Live firing, though, was not taken so seriously as target practice at the academy had been; everyone seemed to keep a playful heart about it, and no one guessed that one day it would really be put to use.

Carrier pigeons—we called this course "raising pigeons"; it was lectured by an instructor Huang, who also demonstrated such things as message-carrying. This instructor Huang was said to be an expert too.

Biochemistry—the main thing was expounding the properties of drugs, such as anesthetics, stimulants, and asphyxiants. Trials were made on a rabbit too, but who would have thought this rabbit was hard to kill: given one injection, it jumped about for the longest while and would not die, to the great embarrassment of the instructor.
The academic subjects and their instructors were roughly as follows:
Military Intelligence Science—lectured by Mr. Zheng Jiemin; the noted book published later, *Military Intelligence Science*, is this very one.

Reconnaissance Method—taught by an officer in charge from the Second Bureau, its content mostly compiled from cases openly published in the First World War. Even then it was felt to be rather out of date.

Communications Method—this took in wireless telegraphy, ciphers, secret writing, secret speech, and the like. A few practice sessions were made, just touching on each; being mostly specialized technique, in a short training it could only be so.

Intelligence Collection—this was a very practical course, with practice too; the whole operation from getting word to submitting a report had to be mastered. But the early exercises, set beside those of today, were a jack-of-all-trades, a thing neither fish nor fowl.
Action and Demolition—weighted toward theory. The instructor who taught this course did not necessarily have practical experience either.

Armed Struggle and Mass Insurrection—this course fixed its eye on the two sides, attack and defense, of the fight against the bandits; Mr. Ye Daoxin compiled the lecture notes himself, then dissected them in fine detail. It was so well taught that it won the whole class's unanimous praise.

Secret Societies—expounding the origins of the Sandianhui, the Gelaohui, the Green Gang, and the Red (Hong) Gang. In truth, secret-society activity was fading day by day, and a little understanding was enough.
The Work of the Cheka—there was a booklet, translated out of Russian, on the secret-service work of Soviet Russia. It sounded rather new to hear in those days.

Higher Police—lectured by our team leader, Mr. Li Shizhen; clear and well-ordered, and much hard work went into it. Could one really apply that set of methods he expounded to public-security work, it would surely bring great effect.
The above are what I can recall; there must be no few I have left out, and it is a great fault that the honored names of many of the instructors are more than I can now supply.

What made a deep impression was that every instructor had a high enthusiasm; lateness or absence was well-nigh unheard of, and they answered questions without wearying of the detail—a rare thing indeed in a training body. And so the general run of classmates listened even to what they did not wish to hear, and made shift to learn even what they could not.

It is a pity that many of the courses were too specialized: rather than learn so many tricks in six months, even to learn but one or two would not necessarily bring one into the inner room and win a "mastery." Still, the good of it was that every trainee could form a notion of "secret-service work," and that may be reckoned as reaching the aim of the training.
In sum, the general run of classmates had their minds not on learning skills; everyone longed to try his hand at the first chance.

Having answered the call-up to join the training, and been entrusted with seeking out the classmates, I thus became the "class monitor" as a matter of course. By "class monitor" is not meant the head of the whole class; apart from leading all the classmates into the classroom, or standing at the head of the ranks, I was, as at any other school, also the class leader the whole body of classmates had elected. At the two roll-calls, morning and evening, it was I who reported the numbers to the team leader; and at each lesson it was I who called the commands—rise, be seated—as the instructor came and went. My place was at the table nearest the platform, the first thing one saw on entering the classroom, so that even to shirk was out of the question.

This was only the surface; underneath, in secret, I had yet another mission. A few days before the training began, Mr. Dai Yunong charged me that I must, in all earnest, do one thing: in the first three months of the training I must set down in writing the thoughts, the words, and every matter worth noting of every classmate, and secretly furnish them to him for his reference—and it must not be known to the other classmates. It was then agreed that he would appoint the adjutant Jia Jinnan, whom I knew, to come and collect them once each Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

Mr. Dai Yunong added: "Should any grave incident arise in the class, you may go to the instruction section and get in touch with the two comrades Zheng Jiemin or Cen Jiazhuo, and telephone me at once." What sort of incident Mr. Dai meant by "grave incident" was not clear to me. I found it very strange: if one day such a thing really happened, would it not be enough to report it to Mr. Zheng Jiemin for him to pass on? Why, then, must it go through Mr. Zheng's channel—that is, get Mr. Zheng's leave for me to telephone out—before I reported to him directly? Of all this I understood little; perhaps Mr. Dai had his own reasons, for he never liked people to question him much, and even when questioned would sometimes answer with silence.

Once the training began, I made the investigation reports as he wished. But at the very start I met a small difficulty: the notebooks the class issued us were barely enough to begin with, and to tear a page or two from each did not yet show, while to tear more might, if discovered, bring on trouble. Apart from drawing on the notebooks, blank paper fit for use was not easy to find. In the end I reported it to Mr. Dai, and it was settled when the man who came, Jia Jinnan, brought in two pads of airmail paper. Small as this matter was, it shows that in anything at all, want of forethought will never do.

Our round of life and work was tightly packed from the first, with little slack in between. And I, being class leader besides, had many routine forms to fill in each day; to find, on top of that, a little more time to write things was truly no easy matter. However much I racked my brains, I could only write a little at a time, by stealth and in scraps.

Think of it: apart from myself, the whole class was twenty-nine men, and by the items Mr. Dai had laid down, even writing plainly and to the point, each man came to two or three hundred words at least, and as much as six or seven hundred at most, so that all told, on an average reckoning, it came to some 15,000 characters in all—and this, moreover, was no essay one might spin out at will and hand in. In writing this sort of report one could neither be slipshod nor harbor the least private bias; for I understood keenly that one word of praise or blame was enough to bear on a man's far-reaching future, and so one should set brush to paper with care, striving to hold to a single fairness.

To be a trainee, one's daily studies were already quite heavy enough; to become class leader loaded on far more than the common classmate carried; and to have to write this investigation report on top of that was to be run off one's feet indeed. Yet, for a full understanding of the classmates under training, I had of necessity to draw closer to every one of them, win their goodwill, and leave no trace of it—no simple thing at all. And so, three months of this wore me half to death; had it not been for a young man's high spirits and my keenness to do well, I could scarcely have borne up.

The business of writing the investigation reports did not go wholly as I would have wished, and there was an episode in it besides: because I often, alone, at the times when I should have rested, did not go back to the dormitory to rest but stayed in the classroom writing with my head down, and yet did not look to be tidying notes or doing lessons, I drew team leader Li's notice; and though he never questioned me to my face, he kept a close watch on me and would not let go. At this I was at a loss. In the end I wrote a little slip of paper and reported the truth to Mr. Dai, and only so was the watch on me lifted. In such a case, from the standpoint of intelligence work, one may count it as having had one's identity exposed.

To speak, again, of getting on with the classmates during the training: on the whole it might be called a general harmony, the chief reason being that no one had any clash of interest, and, added to that, there was no spare time at all; even if there was some small private friction, hemmed in by circumstance it could not rub up into anything. There is a further layer, and I may as well blow my own trumpet a little: being the class leader the men had elected, then, without claiming to be a model to the whole body, I had at least, even for appearance's sake, to keep myself straight. Happily my regular marks were graded A, and in the ordinary practice tests I seldom made a fool of myself, so that the classmates thought well enough of me; and so, seen and unseen, I too worked some harmonizing effect.

Most important, and most to the point, is that besides having an equal chance with the other classmates in the matter of the training, in living conditions I was exactly the same as they. Though I was class monitor and had a personal connection with Mr. Dai Yunong who presided over the training, I had not the least privilege. Whatever others might think, and whatever they might say behind my back, my heart was quite at ease—which is the point on which I feel my ground firmest.

The six months were fast slipping by. Before graduation, each classmate filled in, as required, a work-preference form, one column of which was for the place of work—that is, where one hoped to be posted in future. Reaching this column, I wrote without hesitation the two words "Hangzhou"; this was no last-minute decision, but a longing I had set my heart on long before.

On this point Mr. Dai had specially questioned me; what he valued was whether I had some special working line in Hangzhou, or some plan already in view. At the time it flustered me, and for a moment I could not answer. The true reason was of the subconscious kind: my ancestral home being Hangzhou, a man—and above all one whose thinking is half new and half old—can hardly help harboring the traditional clan feeling; and then I was drawn a little by the saying "Above there is heaven; below, Suzhou and Hangzhou"—which, in truth, had nothing to do with the work.

On graduation day a simple ceremony was held, and the Leader came three times to exhort us, with much of encouragement in his words. Besides all the teaching staff from the director and deputy director on down being present in full, there were, more than at the two previous times, several men of high rank in full arms and well accoutred, whom I did not know. It was said these senior officers had a duty connection with the "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics" newly set up under the Military Affairs Commission in September of that year.

The "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission" mentioned here is what people later called the "Juntong." But the "Juntong" as it really was, the writer would presume to divide into two stages, early and late; the "Juntong" of this moment ought to be the "early Juntong," for at that time the Bureau was divided into three departments, and Mr. Dai Yunong was responsible for only one of them, namely the "Second Department." Not until 1938, after the outbreak of the War of Resistance, was the "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics" reorganized, with He Yaozu as nominal chief and Dai Li presiding over the whole bureau's work as deputy chief—and this is the formal "Juntong." On this foundation, through several changes of name, though the "system" is no more, its working spirit has carried on to this day. It is what is now the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense.

That evening the whole class dined together; the director and deputy director both stayed away, and Mr. Dai Yunong presided over all as their representative. The dinner over, individual talks were held in the class headquarters office, Mr. Dai Yunong and Mr. Zheng Jiemin summoning us in turn. It was only last that my turn came to speak with Mr. Dai; he gave me some special words of encouragement, and appointed me to come the next morning to No. 53 Ji'e Lane for a talk.
By this time I had known Dai Yunong exactly one year. From then on we were partners in the work; in the relation of superior to subordinate, he was my chief and I his man.

In the assignment of work, Mr. Dai did not consider my wish to go to Hangzhou; he had already decided to send me to Beiping to found the work. As for Beiping, it was my second home, where I was born and where I grew up, and should have been dearer to me than Hangzhou; so of course I was glad of it in my heart. Going with me—that is, sent out together—were also Yang Ying and Qi Nanpu, the two who had trained together with us. Though I was appointed to take charge, at that time there was as yet no fixed establishment, so it was not clearly laid down that I was the "group leader" among the three.

I remember very clearly: there was nothing whatever in writing; what work I was assigned, what mission I bore, rested on Mr. Dai's word alone. Had he written out a slip besides, it was only handed to the personnel department for registration, and the man concerned might not even see what was written on that slip. It was thus, "without a scrap of proof," that I joined the "secret-service work."

A word I had bottled up, I at last one day brought myself to ask Mr. Dai. I said: "I have already joined the 'Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association'—you have long known this, Mr. Dai?" Mr. Dai answered straight: "It was brother Huang Jianqiu who nominated and introduced you; he has told me of it." Only then did I grasp that it was brother Jianqiu who had introduced me—though he had never once mentioned the matter to me.

I asked Mr. Dai again: "How does our work stand in relation to the 'Military Association'? Are they one thing, or two?" He was silent a long while and said nothing, and after another moment said only, "You will come to understand it in time"—a wide-of-the-mark reply like that. At the time I was much displeased at heart: I held that where there is a question there should be an answer, and that he ought in reason to explain it to me plainly. Only later did I come to see that, because there was this layer of the "Lixingshe" in it, and I was but a "member" beneath the "Lixingshe," the organization was bound to keep it from me, so that he could not explain it to me.

Before I set out, Mr. Dai held besides a farewell gathering for me alone, chiefly to make me acquainted with several comrades in charge of inside work; present were brothers Xu Weibin, Lin Huan, Zhang Gunfu, and others. The feast over, Mr. Dai made me a gift of a Browning pistol. That pistol was short and thick, of large bore, its make not to be told; some said it was Italian-made. As he handed me the pistol, he stressed once more that this was a personal gift for a keepsake, and hoped I would keep it long. Who would have guessed that this pistol would truly "startle all with its first cry" and "sound out beyond the common," and, in its maiden trial, be put to great use?
Checking the dates and the exact time, the finishing of training and the sending-out ought to have been between November and December 1932.

Writing to this point, I may as well repeat what was said before and speak of the truth of the "Juntong" and the "Lixingshe." In the past there were many rumors, and not only outsiders but even some of those in the organization could not necessarily tell the one clearly from the other; below I first give a general explanation, and the detailed inside story I shall reflect as it truly was in the several volumes of the whole *Nameless Heroes*.

In March 1932 the "Lixingshe" was founded at Nanjing. On the first of April that same year was formed the "Special Services Department" under Dai Li. For a time it was also called the "Sixth Department"; afterward, the name "Sixth Department" is no longer to be seen in the documents.

In March 1932 the National Government set up the Military Affairs Commission, and in September of that year, under the Military Affairs Commission, established the "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics," the "Juntong" for short. This body was not made public, so few outside knew of it; Dai Li was appointed head of the bureau's "Second Department."

On the surface, though the "Special Services Department" belonging to the "Lixingshe" and the "Second Department" belonging to the "Juntong" were under different lines of subordination, in fact they were two faces of one body. For example, the two had but a single place of office, and the "Intelligence Section" under the "Special Services Department" was the very same as the "Intelligence Section" under the "Second Department," and so on.

From 1932 down to Mr. Dai Yunong's death in 1946, and even for some years after Mr. Dai's death, the "secret-service work" he led and founded took shape, it cannot be denied, into a powerful "system." This system, on the Chinese political scene, once went beyond its own working sphere and worked a certain measure of political effect. This would take a special volume to set out thoroughly; here I touch on it only in brief, and shall treat it in detail hereafter.
To speak fairly and judge by the facts, the doings of the "Juntong" did indeed make a great contribution to the nation; though, of course, no one would dare say there was not one small blemish.

To go on further: the "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission" set up in September 1932 was a non-established unit of the earlier period, and who was the bureau's chief no one, in the several decades since, has ever mentioned; there are of course some rumors, mostly without any proof, and now there is no one left to verify it. So far as I personally know, the bureau, besides Bureau Head Dai Li's "Second Department," of course also had a "First Department," which, I have heard, was headed by a man sent from the several central ministries, and may well be what later became the "Zhongtong." Nor was it only the First and Second Departments; there was besides a "Third Department," whose head was Chen Zhuo, a former chief of the Capital Police Department. Whether this is exactly so I dare not warrant, and I respectfully await the guidance of those in the know.

By 1938 the reorganized "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics" had been formally brought into the establishment, still under the Military Affairs Commission. He Yaozu took the post of bureau chief, and Dai Li bore the real responsibility as deputy chief. Why He Yaozu should hold an empty title, there must be a reason, only we do not know it; if one is to guess, it may be that Dai Yunong's standing was not deep enough.

As for the name "Special Services Department," it was probably abolished in 1938, at the same time as the "Lixingshe" and the "Renaissance Society" were transformed and reorganized into the "Three People's Principles Youth Corps"—or perhaps a little earlier in time. That is to say, by 1938 the secret-service work Mr. Dai presided over was no longer that two-faces-of-one-body state of things. Yet, as need required, many new bodies were established one after another outside the "Juntong," and all of them too were Mr. Dai's responsibility.
For fear of straying on too long and wandering ever further from the point, on this matter of the mutual relation of the "Juntong" and the "Lixingshe," I write only to here.
To take up the former thread, I speak again of matters bearing on the Honggongci Special Service Police Training Class.

The first term of the Honggongci Special Service Police Class had, at its opening, thirty trainees in all. Midway, a student named Zeng left off his studies for some cause; and afterward two more withdrew through illness, so that by the time of graduation and assignment there were only twenty-seven.

Where all twenty-seven classmates were assigned, I never wholly knew; and in work of our kind it does not do to ask too much. Yet, our friendships being deep, there were those who privately passed word to one another. For instance, Liao Zongze of Hangzhou and I often corresponded in friendship. So far as I know, besides Yang Ying and Qi Nanpu who went to Beiping with me, four classmates—Weng Yikui, Zhuang Junlie, Wang Yishi, and Tang Huanwen—were later added to the "Beiping Station" work.

Two years later, that is in 1934, when I attended meetings and was received in audience at Nanjing and Mount Lu, I chanced to meet classmates Liu Yiguang at Nanjing, Liao Zongze at Hangzhou, Tian Dongyun in Sichuan, and Zheng Xingzhou at Zhengzhou. As to what work they did in those places, I understood little.

Through several upheavals and changes, of those who came to Taiwan after 1949 there were eight in all; the rest, who stayed on the mainland, are, to speak roughly, I suppose no longer in the world. Of those I have word of: Qi Nanpu was struggled to death by the Chinese Communists long ago in his native Quanjiao County in Anhui; Weng Yikui fell in battle against the Communist army at Laohekou—but of the dates of both I know nothing. As for the others, the Intelligence Bureau may now have records and know something; I have not gone to inquire, but would that they were still alive and well.
A few years ago classmate Weng Guanghui, after enduring the utmost from a stroke, died in Taiwan.
Down to the end of May 1981, seven were still living in Taiwan:
Yu Yaoli, of Jiangxi, fifth class of the Military Academy, delegate to the National Assembly, in poor health, once operated on for emphysema.
Chen Zhijing, of Henan, fifth class of the Military Academy. Once a Taipei city councillor, suffering from arthritis.

Liu Yiguang, of Hunan, fourth class of the Military Academy. For several decades he was in attendance on Zhang Xueliang, rising step by step from major to major general. Now retired, close on eighty, he no longer moves about easily.
Qiu Yaoxun, of Fujian, sixth class of the Military Academy. To this day hale in body, past seventy yet like a man of fifty; still, he is busy about his living.

Yang Ying, of Hunan, sixth class of the Military Academy. Once education chief of the Infantry School, long since retired; now he copies calligraphy models and tends flowers, dandling his grandchildren—the most fortunate of men.
Zhuang Junlie, of Fujian, fifth class of the Military Academy. Bedridden with a stroke for years now, still struggling on with life.

Chen Gongshu, of Hebei, fifth class of the Military Academy. A whole life of folly—the good-for-nothing is the writer himself. By Heaven's care, when I should have died I did not, and this life was left me.
Now I do nothing at all, but with a single mind write out this book, *Nameless Heroes*.

Of the seven men above, the youngest is seventy-two, the eldest seventy-eight or nine; the circumstances of each are all different, and could they be written out, each would make a fine story rich in the stuff of legend.

Usually, when a body of men have trained together in one class, at the moment of graduation and parting they ought to leave an address, or take a group photograph for a keepsake; we did none of this, no one telling another where he was now bound, not even saying, "Till we meet again." Could it be that this was the parting of the ways, each to go his own road? The managing staff instructed us all: "This is the nature of our work."

The higher-ups decided to send Yang Ying, Qi Nanpu, and me, three men, to Beiping to found the work. To fit ourselves out with clothes we were held up a few more days. The weather was already turning cool, and we had thought to dress in a way that fitted our station, but the clothing allowance was truly pitiful; cover the head, and we could not cover the foot—truly, as the saying goes, patching the elbow only tore the shoulder—and we ended looking a sorry, ill-assorted lot instead.

For travel money too we could only take third-class carriages, and on ordinary passenger-and-freight trains the journey took three days and three nights; ill-fed and ill-slept, we ended every one of us disheveled and grimy, in a wretched plight.
On reaching Tianjin, Yang Ying and Qi Nanpu changed trains and went straight on to Beiping, while I was to stop and make contact with one man and see to two matters.

I had once stayed in Tianjin at the Liyuan Inn, set up on Hebei Avenue, and, not knowing other quarters, this time found the same place again. Had I put up at a great hotel in the Concessions, then even had I money enough, I dare say I should not have ventured in.

The man I was to contact was the person in charge of the Tianjin area; the higher-ups told me his name was Zheng Shisong—surely a cover name. The address was in a quiet residential quarter of the British Concession, a good long way from Hebei Avenue, and I changed cars two or three times before I found it.

He came to the door in person, and, before I could open my mouth, seemed already to know who I was. I gave my name, and he too asked no more, but very warmly bade me come in and sit. And so we made contact quite naturally, without in fact any of that business of passwords and hand-signs.
The parlor was quite splendidly furnished, and even the small ornaments for decoration had all been choicely and cleverly picked; but they looked to carry, more or less, an Eastern flavor.

This Zheng Shisong was a fine figure of a man, of middling build and regular features, without a single distinguishing mark to be found on him from head to foot. A pair of large eyes, full of spirit, only the gaze unsettled—a man, it may be, of much settled purpose. He wore the newest of narrow-legged Western suits, square-toed leather shoes with cloth gaiter-covers, a high-collared white shirt, a silk figured necktie—a most particular gentleman's air. Set the two of us side by side, my own turnout, though it need not have been ashamed of itself, yet showed shabby.

We had scarcely fallen to talking, before three sentences were out, than it came clear how green I was. He was sixteen years my senior; I was but new from the shell, while he was already seasoned in the ways of the world.

Mr. Zheng Shisong's true surname was Wang, his original name Renqiang; after entering the work he changed his name to Wang Tianmu. His schooling and career took in the Baoding officers' academy, a Japanese military academy, service as an adviser in the Northwest Army, and the taking-in of bandits about Henan, where he once styled himself commander—and so on. For talent and learning he had truly a bellyful, and even the few characters he wrote were fit to hang on a plaque; a remarkable man indeed.

He was an old friend of Mr. Dai Yunong's; they had a deep friendship, and later all but became kin by the marriage of their children. Before Mr. Dai had yet taken up the "Special Services Department," they had long worked together. He had been sent to found the work in Tianjin half a year before we went to Beiping, and at this time the work in Tianjin was already on quite a scale.

What I stopped in Tianjin to ask his help with was the matter of how to send telegrams once I reached Beiping. In those days the work under Mr. Dai, whether the "Special Services Department" or the "Second Department," had no wireless equipment of its own, and a field unit's telegrams to Nanjing had to be sent by the good offices of the Party Central's Investigation Section (?). So it was in Tianjin, and so too in Beiping. Because Tianjin had a link with them, I asked Mr. Zheng Shisong to build me a bridge.

In the ordinary way, field units were not allowed to form lateral ties; this time, on the contrary, it was the higher-ups who wanted our two units at Beiping and Tianjin to keep in close touch. This too was the second matter I had to see to.

Once I had made my errand plain, these two matters were easily concluded and smoothly settled. Mr. Zheng Shisong very earnestly asked me out to a meal, and, unable well to decline, I went at last. Because the place we went was too grand, I could taste nothing at all of the whole meal, minding only that I should on no account make a fool of myself. After the meal Mr. Zheng Shisong sent me back to the inn in his own motorcar. This was our first contact, and he left a deep impression on me, and I liked him well besides.
Beiping is my birthplace, and in my mind, so long as a thing belonged to Beiping, all of it was good, without exception good—good even to the point of doting.

Once my two comrades Yang Ying and Qi Nanpu and I had gathered together, we, as we had talked over on the road, at once took our first step—to find a good place to light on, to settle in, to work from, and to make our start.
Within a day or two, a house such as one might scour the whole four quarters of the city and hardly light on, we actually found; nothing could have suited our conditions better.
The rent was very cheap, needing only payment in advance before moving in, and not even a deposit.
This house stood on a great street open on every side, most convenient for coming and going.
Of usable rooms there were but two and a half; but the good of it was that it was a house apart with its own gate and court, and, the gate shut, no one could see what deviltry we were up to inside.
Unlooked-for, the landlord had a telephone installed and did not mean to move away; we had only to return him the telephone deposit, and it was ours to use.
Of course there is no perfect thing under heaven: this house had no bath, and the privy was too filthy besides.

Yang Ying and I are neither of us superstitious; never minding whether the day was lucky or ill, we moved in first and talked afterward. Qi Nanpu was willing to take the field work, and settled himself separately outside.

None of us had a cover occupation; too clever by half, we hung at the gate a wooden signboard reading "Beiping Branch of the Military Journal Press," fully thinking it could pass for a front, and that, should anyone come to inquire, we could meet the case—little dreaming it would later land us in great trouble.

The police of the substation came too to check the household registration; whatever you said, so he wrote it in the register—easy to deal with; but had he walked into the rooms to look, then, even without showing the cloven hoof, it would likely have roused suspicion. Speaking of the Beiping police substation, it is a most interesting thing, and truly worth saying a few words more about.

For many years the Beiping natives all called the police substation the "gezi"; why it is called "gezi," I have never asked the learned, and dare not talk wildly. But the "gezi" I have seen were, for years, small huts built of planks on an open lot, the outside painted a liver-colored paint, with two little tables set inside, the household registers strung on cords and hung in rows on the wall; the police gentlemen sitting up on a ladder, winter cold or summer heat alike, would carry on their business just so.

For service to the people, the Beiping substations may be reckoned first in the whole country: to look up a name go to the "gezi," for a brawl or a fight up to the "gezi," to report a birth or a death to the "gezi," a quarrel between mother- and daughter-in-law or a squabble among sisters-in-law also troubles the "gezi"—anything you cannot settle yourself, there is nothing you may not take to the "gezi." Even what he cannot deal with, he will yet answer you with a kind face and untiring patience, never lording it over you or keeping you off at a distance.

Just because the Beiping police were close to the residents, they could know eight or nine parts of the state of every household in their district. If one must find a weak point, it was the lack of political sense.
Once we had a fixed working address, besides reporting it to the higher-ups for the record, we also gave word to Zheng Shisong in Tianjin, that we might take up the mutual link.

We began to learn the use of the cipher book brought from Nanjing, and sent out our first telegram; Yang Ying served as code clerk, and I doubled as "courier," carrying this draft telegram to Suzhou Hutong in the east city and handing it to "Mr. Zhang" of "Zhang Pei"—"Zhang Pei," I suppose, being a cover name, and being also the wireless station of the Party Central's Investigation Section at Beiping. The time we relied on them to send our telegrams was very brief; by the beginning of 1933 the higher-ups sent the wireless specialist comrade Cheng Jun to Beiping, and set up a station of our own for our exclusive use.

In the early days of our vigorously opening up the work, short of hands, pinched for funds, and, on top of that, with no working experience at all, the four words "nothing to boast of" fit us most aptly.
By February 1933, with our working array a little strengthened, we then gradually pressed forward one small step.

In the matter of personnel, those who joined the inside work were Bai Shiwei, a seventh-class academy classmate introduced by Qi Nanpu, and Wang Yunsun, recommended by Wang Zhaohuai, a veteran comrade of the bureau headquarters. Neither of these two performed any rite or procedure in joining the work; being introduced by comrades of our own, they were treated from the outset as basic comrades.
The intelligence contacts taken in on the spot (whom we called internally "handled personnel") were three: Hou Zichuan, Zhang Bowu, and Fan Xing.

Zhang Bowu was recommended by Mr. Zheng Shisong of Tianjin, and Hou Zichuan in turn brought in by Zhang Bowu. The two of them were originally of the Youth Party, though at the time I did not know it. Hou Zichuan gradually owned to it; Zhang Bowu would never admit it to the end. What Zhang and Hou supplied was all local intelligence, of limited working value; now and then there was some data on the movements of the Northeast Army too, but that was of no account either.

Fan Xing, courtesy name Jiman, of Sichuan, claimed to be of the sixth class of the Central Military Academy; at this time he was also reading at the "Art Academy" in Beiping and studying painting. This gentleman could truly be called a figure of legend.

Our meeting too was quite by chance.
