One day I went to see Jiang Tian (Lisheng), a classmate of my own enlisted company, newly come to Beiping from his native Yutian County in East Hebei and lodging for the time at the home of his elder cousin Jiang Yunqing. Jiang Yunqing's father, named Jiang Hao, was an old-line Communist ranked with Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu, who had died years before at Vladivostok. Jiang Yunqing had two younger sisters besides, the second Yiqing, the third Taiqing, both of somewhat leftist leaning. Fan Xing was the boyfriend of the third sister, Jiang Taiqing.

The Jiang house was small, and we all crowded together to chat. Fan Xing was not only a good talker, but everything he said was to the point; we were all held by his voice and manner. I thought: here is a capable hand, and I must draw him in whatever it takes. This notion once born, after a few comings and goings, he thus became our intelligence man.

At the start it was nothing much, but afterward it gained ground more and more, and the intelligence he supplied grew ever more important, such as: Japan's military dispositions in China, and the Japanese military's political intrigues; the exchange of understandings among the powers over Japan's aggression against China, and other high-grade intelligence. The source, by Fan's report, was an interpreter in the military attaché's office of a certain country's embassy in China—but we never once saw this man. At the time I personally had not yet the ability to judge intelligence of this kind, and so passed it all on as it came; and the reaction of the higher-ups was that it was "of considerable reference value" too.

This was the beginning of our gathering of important intelligence, and may be called, too, a strange encounter in the course of intelligence work; but the development of the matter was not so simple, and there were in it many doubtful points that could not be broken through.
Besides this, the two the higher-ups assigned me merely to keep in touch with (only to keep contact, with no power to direct) were Liao Huaping and a certain Yu (whose name I have forgotten).

Mr. Liao Huaping had, in his academy days, been one of our political instructors—I recall he taught "History of Social Evolution"—and I could never have thought that we should meet again in such a case. Mr. Liao had been a delegate to the First National Congress of the Chinese Kuomintang, and also a member of the First Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party—a man of very old standing. In the party purge of 1927 Liao Huaping fled from Guangzhou, slipped into Beiping to carry on activity, and was arrested by the Beiping Gendarmerie Command. Repenting his former errors and willing to work for us, he was handed over to be kept in contact by the unit Mr. Dai had stationed at Beiping. Mr. Liao later held such posts as director of the inspectorate of the "Bureau of Confidential Investigation," and died in Taiwan in 1952.

The certain Yu's history was much like Mr. Liao Huaping's, his standing quite deep too. By 1935 and 1936, when this man surnamed Yu held a post in the "Bandit-Suppression Headquarters for the three provinces of Henan, Hubei, and Anhui," he was found stealing secret documents, arrested a second time, and executed.

In March 1933 the higher-ups ordered us to draw up a budget, in which were such items as living expenses, operating expenses, office expenses, and special expenses. The sum approved was about three thousand-odd yuan. My own "living and operating expenses" came to some three hundred-odd yuan, not reckoned separately, with a further "special expense" of one hundred, coming to four hundred-odd in all—no small sum indeed. I can still remember clearly that fine foreign white flour then sold at only two yuan eight jiao a sack; converted at today's rate in Taiwan, the four hundred-odd yuan of 1933 comes to about 50,000-odd yuan of 1981—and even if there be some difference, it will not be far off.
The name "Beiping Station" was probably fixed from about this time. Yet there was no commission, no assignment, still less any express notice; but it held good all the same.
The work of the "Beiping Station" had no definite prescription; at that time, apart from gathering intelligence, there was nothing else we could really do.

The unrest of the times and the shifts of the political scene affected us too. On 11 March 1933 the topmost man in Beiping, Zhang Xueliang, announced his retirement by open telegram. On the 12th, General He Yingqin took the post of acting chairman of the Beiping Branch of the Military Affairs Commission. The North China situation, pressed by Japan, grew tenser still.
Mr. Zheng Jiemin, too, was posted to Beiping at this time.

Mr. Zheng's coming bore a grave mission and carried multiple identities besides. In the way of secret-service work, he was the immediate superior of our "Beiping Station," being the "special commissioner" the Military Affairs Commission's "Bureau of Investigation and Statistics" had stationed in the North China region, his jurisdiction taking in Chahar, Suiyuan, and the Northeast; at the same time he was assistant of the "Special Services Department" belonging to the "Lixingshe," in position second only to Mr. Dai Yunong.
Besides this double identity, Mr. Zheng held yet another post in the Third Bureau of the General Staff Headquarters—that being the formal military office, wearing arms and uniform and bearing rank.

By what I understood, on the side of the secret organization "Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People," Mr. Zheng was also the highest man in charge stationed in North China. Under what title, I cannot say; but I had private dealings with fellow student Jia Yi, secretary of the "Beiping branch of the Lixingshe," and Mr. Zheng's position must have stood above the branch secretary's, from which I judge he may have been the "special commissioner" or the secretary of the "North China Branch." Under Mr. Zheng Jiemin's charge were two assistant secretaries, one Wang Renyuan, the other Qi Qingbin. Qi Qingbin will appear many times in this book, *Nameless Heroes*, and in the end he too became one of our "nameless heroes."

Though I was a member of the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association," the second-tier body under the leadership of the "Lixingshe," I had never once taken part in its organizational activity. I did not know that the "Revolutionary Soldiers' Comrades Association" had already been dissolved and reorganized and merged into the "Revolutionary Youth Comrades Association," nor did I receive any notice transferring my membership from the "Military Association" to the "Youth Association."

Mr. Zheng Jiemin worked out of two places. One was on Fuyou Street near Zhongnanhai—this was the "special commissioner's office" of the Juntong's Second Department, which had a direct bearing on our work; helping Mr. Zheng handle his daily affairs there was a comrade Xing Shan (Senzhou). The other was of the "Lixingshe" organization, and I went there too.

Ever since Mr. Zheng came, the link between the "Beiping Station" and the Nanjing bureau headquarters was markedly reduced; save for personnel and funds, in all such matters as work guidance and the handling of intelligence we took our orders straight from Mr. Zheng—that is, in the working system, one more layer had been added above the "Beiping Station."

As for the "Beiping Station's" working position being lowered a notch, we took it as a need of the working disposition and felt nothing else about it; whatever the higher-ups decided, we followed—the more so as, toward Mr. Zheng's enlightened leadership, everyone was thoroughly content.

Mr. Zheng was generous by nature and treated his subordinates as his own sons and younger brothers; the longer one was with him, the more one came to relish that genuine warmth of feeling. He was from Wenchang in Guangdong, of the second class of the Whampoa Academy, had studied in Russia, and had a high grounding in modern military science; later he was especially versed in international affairs. At that time he was also the only man who had studied the theoretical system of "secret-service work."

Mr. Zheng took a special interest in the intelligence data gathered through Fan Xing, and summoned Fan Xing many times to exchange views on that source of intelligence, though he never got a satisfying answer. On this matter Mr. Zheng instructed me apart: "Fan Xing's intelligence is high in quality, but its reliability is uneven; if we cannot get thoroughly to the truth of the source, there will still be misgivings in putting the intelligence to use hereafter."
Mr. Zheng pointed out further: "By Fan Xing's past intelligence, it is very unlikely that so much could be got from one and the same source."

Mr. Zheng's meaning was that, though Fan Xing's intelligence was not poor in quality, if we did not know just how it was got—where on earth it came from—then, because we had our doubts, we dared not rashly put it to actual use. This was my responsibility, and I had, by Mr. Zheng's instruction, to make a fuller, many-sided inquiry into Fan Xing.

Fan Xing lived alone near the "Art Academy" in Beiping, in a small room with only a table and a bed. Such houses were let expressly to students, at a rent of only some three or four yuan a month. One day I paid him a special call, meaning to chat more with him and improve my understanding. Unlooked-for, there was another girl in the room besides—call her a girl, but she was in fact over twenty. Fan Xing introduced her as his fellow student Peng Yaluo, also a fellow provincial from Sichuan; and by the look of things the two were somewhat abashed, as though they were more than merely fellow students and fellow provincials. I thought to myself: if this Peng Yaluo too is Fan Xing's sweetheart, then was there not still that Jiang Taiqing at the Jiang house?
This was but one doubtful point, and could not answer any question; whether it had any bearing on what I wanted to know was not yet certain.

Some days later, I went alone to stroll in the Dong'an Market and, wandering to the bookstalls of the Dangui Bazaar, turned over this and looked at that, meaning to buy a few books too. Speaking of the Dangui Bazaar, it too was a relic of the Beiping of old: the Dangui Bazaar was a part of the Dong'an Market, on the side near Wangfujing Avenue, several hundred feet in length, just like a street. Roofed within, so that it minded neither wind nor rain, it had on both sides nothing but bookshops and stationers, and down the middle of the way too were spread bookstalls long and short, leaving only two narrow passages, left and right, for people to walk. On the stalls and in the shops, books and journals of every character were all to be had; among them some sold thread-bound books only, some only new literary works, and it was no rarity for one stall to sell besides several kinds of journal of differing political stripe. If a man wanted to buy some banned book of the far left, he would fetch it out too, from a crack between the piled books or from a wooden cabinet, to meet the market; and there were a few shops more improper still that sold even lewd books and pictures just the same, and who seemed very skilled at reading faces, telling at a glance who was a real buyer and who a detective "looking for trouble."

Choosing at the stalls no book I wished to buy, and just in the act of picking over this and that, I raised my head and saw the direct courier of the "Beiping Station," Fan Xing, just then coming out of a bookshop on the slant. In his hand he held a small roll of something—I could not make out clearly what it was—and when he in turn caught sight of me, he hurriedly stuffed the roll into the pocket of his short overcoat, and, while walking toward me, kept glancing back over his shoulder; his mouth made small talk as he put out his hand to shake mine, but the look on his face, flushing red then white, showed very unnatural. I felt: "This fellow surely has something to hide."

I very much wanted to snatch the roll from his pocket and see just what it was; but had I done so, would it not have made things awkward, and what then of the second step? Better to feign not having seen, and pay out the line long, and deal with it later.
Fan Xing perhaps had his own reckoning; from then on what he showed seemed more active than before, more fitted to the needs of the work. By reason and sense, this was not a normal thing.

For his sake the "Beiping Station" put in no little effort too—frontal, flanking, and covert alike; but the result was still that what could be affirmed was little, and what stayed in doubt was much, and it was very hard to reach a judgment.

What we did come to understand of him was this: he was versed in the scripts of several countries, English and Russian, able both to write and to speak them. In his everyday talk, what hung on his lips were all words to do with literature and art, and on his table and by his bed were set all books of that same kind, only he never once talked politics.

He said he studied painting at the "Art Academy," yet his work was never seen; on inquiring at the "Art Academy," it was true enough—there was such a man, who had registered and often went in, but seldom attended lessons.

He often went to such foreign-flavored places as the Beijing Hotel and the German Hotel, seeming to be looking for someone more than sitting down to eat, and it was never found that he had contact with anyone—which was always felt to be very strange.
The intelligence he reported he insisted was got from the "military attaché's office" of a certain country in the legation district, yet he was never seen going in and out of the "Legation Quarter."

Then how did the stuff of this "military attaché's office" come to hand? Was it "made up" by himself, and then fitted out with a borrowed source? That could not be either, for a part of the intelligence he reported was afterward confirmed.

Time and again we asked to know this man who supplied the intelligence and called himself "Huang Runsheng," to meet him once; Fan Xing always said the man would not. We asked again that Fan Xing bring the man somewhere, anywhere, and point him out to us, promising on no account to speak with him; and Fan Xing, though he agreed by word of mouth to try to arrange it, always put us off with "there has been no chance," and dragged it out again and again.

Fan Xing's two sweethearts—Jiang Taiqing and Peng Yaluo—were neither of them simple; whether they were truly making love there, or had some other use, could not for the moment be decided; but it seemed to have no connection with our work.
What on earth was Fan Xing after? Could it be only for that paltry sum of a few hundred yuan? If the true aim lay in money, we reckoned this a very good bargain—it likely could not be so simple.
I laid all this data before Mr. Zheng Jiemin and discussed it with him; he thought the matter not hard to handle, and set out several principles of handling at the same time:
"If it is for money, we can satisfy him accordingly; what should be spent, spare not;

"Supposing he has some political background or international connection, that is just the working lead we could ask for; there is no harm in playing along with his game and carrying on a testing 'intelligence war' and 'political struggle';

"As for certain doubtful points, do not press to solve them at once, for so far we have suffered no loss whatever. From now on we should observe coolly, and on no account provoke him in word or act; best to build up a personal feeling with him, which will work a steadying effect;

"With the intelligence he passes on, we must from now on handle it carefully, keeping the originals, for concentrated review and comparison of the earlier with the later." This matter was done as Mr. Zheng directed, and we shall await its later development.

My relations with Fan Xing thus began, and were kept up off and on, in "friendship," for a full twenty-one years. Not until the spring of 1949, just before I was to leave Shanghai, was this riddle-gourd at last opened. Yet it was not finished, and there is a sequel—that being a matter of 1953 in Hong Kong. These strange plots past all compare I shall set out one by one in what follows.
Do not make light of him: he was a man with quite a "background." Guess if you can—what was his true identity?
The foregoing account looks somewhat trifling; but in fact, at the founding of the work, it was indeed a jumble without order.

At the beginning of April 1933, Mr. Dai Yunong came to Beiping to inspect the work, with his confidential secretary Mao Wanli and a party of several including a code clerk. In fact he had other, higher-level activity besides.

After Mr. Dai reached Beiping, at first he lodged alone at the Beijing Hotel, the rest of his party at the Garden Hotel in the west city. Before long he rented, in a lane off Qifenglou in the east city, a two-storey dwelling with a court, and engaged a cook besides, and so settled in—meaning, I suppose, to make a rather long stay.

As for the true state of the "Beiping Station's" work, there was no need for me to make him a presentation; he already knew it as clearly as the palm of his hand. He had no mind to blame us; what he looked for from us was how vigorously to push the work forward, to strive for a showing.

To speak truly, we few were held back by our social connections not being broad enough and our social standing being too low; in fact many upper-level lines we simply could not attach ourselves to, and, wish as we might to do well, that was easier said than done—it was a thing not to be forced.
How discerning Mr. Dai was; of course he could appreciate this, and his making ready for a long stay at Beiping had much of the intent, too, of taking the field himself and showing his hand.

At this juncture, because the North China situation was pressing, the declining old capital of Beiping suddenly became again a center of military and political weight; for a time the great ones gathered thick, and it was very lively. As to what the military and political chiefs conferred over, our humble little unit could not sense.

On the day after Mr. Dai reached Beiping, the man in charge of the "Tianjin Station," Zheng Shisong (Wang Tianmu), came at his summons. It is said that he and Mr. Dai were old friends, and that even before the "Special Services Department" and the "Second Department" were set up, when Mr. Dai worked in the Personal Staff Office, they had already been partners in secret-service work. The time may be traced back to 1928. Now that there was a fixed working post, all the more must they join efforts and do a great thing.

The range of Mr. Dai and his men's activity was quite wide, reaching into every layer of society. As to its content, apart from the matters I had a part in, there was much I did not know. We had an unwritten rule of principle: what one need not know, one should not ask or hear much of. Yet a man is a man after all; setting aside the thirst for knowledge and curiosity, still, seen and unseen, meant and unmeant, one could not help lending an ear here and casting an eye there.
One tale in it of much interest is how Mr. Dai Yunong came to "strike up ties" with Wu Taixun, one of the "Four Young Masters":

Wu Taixun, courtesy name Youquan, called "the Fifth Master" and not by his name, was the son of Wu Junsheng (Xingquan), the former military governor of Heilongjiang. Wu Junsheng was one of the leading figures "murdered" by the ambitious Japanese soldiery in the "Huanggutun train-bombing plot," dying at the same time as Zhang Zuolin. This "Fifth Master Wu" had never seriously read a day's books, and was a typical young man of fashion; only in the way he dealt with people and affairs, he could earn the four great words "open-handed and fond of righteousness." Though he had inherited the vast fortune his old father left, he was by no means one of those rich men without a conscience.

The tale is that how much property his house held, even he himself could not reckon. Since Mr. Dai and he had long had dealings, I too grew familiar with Wu Youquan. One day, after two cups of wine, in high spirits and half in jest, I asked him: "Your house has so much money—do you know how it came?" He caught my meaning, and, taking no offense, told me: "My father did not scrape it off the land! In the old days the country folk of Heilongjiang all burned as firewood the soybeans they could not eat, thinking it no waste; later, at someone's pointing, they learned they could sell them to foreigners for good money. We bought up the surplus beans from the country folk and sold them on, and that is how the money was laid by." How much truth there is in this account I dare not rashly judge, and can only let it pass. Perhaps this noble young man was so guileless that in his own mind he believed it truly so.

Wu Youquan never did join our work, nor was his name ever formally entered in our internal personnel records. So far as I know, he gave the work under Mr. Dai's leadership real help of many kinds—besides manpower, financial support as well. From April 1932 right down to after the victory in the War of Resistance, whether at Beiping, Shanghai, or Hong Kong, he kept up close comings and goings with Mr. Dai.

Mr. Dai treated this noble young man with much courtesy, and had a real mind to bring him along and temper him, hoping he might do something worthwhile. So during the War of Resistance a plan was once made to send Wu Youquan and our working comrades Li Guochen and Wu Anzhi, following General Li Du, into the Northeast by a roundabout route, to join up a Volunteer Army and work a great thing together. But all were blocked by one cause or another and could not set out.

Unhappily, when Mr. Dai perished in the air crash of 1946, the Juntong kept no more close tie with Wu Youquan. Though Mr. Zheng Jiemin and Mr. Mao Renfeng both had occasional contact with Wu Youquan, it was no longer that close and intimate state of things of Mr. Dai's lifetime.

For Wu Youquan personally, a still unhappier thing befell: in 1948, Wu Youquan's wife, Miss Zhu the Ninth (by name Yuan, ninth sister of Miss Zhu the Fifth, and daughter of Zhu Qiqian, finance minister of the Beiyang government), on a flight to Hong Kong, was killed when the plane struck a mountain. The many precious jewels she carried were all scorched; certain passbooks, receipts, and securities were burnt up too—a truly fatal blow. In matters of money it had always been Miss Zhu the Ninth who kept charge, while Wu Youquan himself understood little; once the accident happened, to make it good again was hard. By Wu Youquan's account, the deposits recovered afterward came to a very limited sum too. From then the family declined, and fell past all recovery.

Wu Youquan lived in reduced straits in Hong Kong a long while, and in 1957 died of liver cancer, aged only forty-odd. At the last he suffered the utmost, so poor that he could not even pay the one hundred Hong Kong dollars a month of his mutual-aid society. To think of it brings a great bitterness. What may console him below is that his two sons are grown to manhood, each with his own attainments.

To speak fairly, Wu Youquan did indeed give the "Juntong" no little help; only it is a pity it was never set down on the "Juntong's" account. Now, with the writer for witness, in my *Nameless Heroes* I count him as a "nameless hero" and pay him my respects.

Of course, Mr. Dai's activity in Beiping was not all built up through Wu Youquan's connection. But following this line of Wu Youquan's, he did indeed come into contact with many worthies and talents of Northeastern origin. Among those I knew were Li Tiancai, Guan Jiyu, Wang Zhuoran, and others. There were besides young officers, serving or retired, such as Wang Yizhe, Yuan Chonggu, and Feng Yong.

Of these men, some later formed working ties, some got no further than a first meeting or the building of a certain measure of tacit understanding. I recall that those Mr. Dai appointed me to keep in touch with were Li Tiancai and Guan Jiyu, two men. The "keeping in touch" here meant passing letters for them and fixing a time of meeting; as to what business they were specifically about, I did not know.

After a while I came gradually to see that Mr. Dai's doings were not confined to intelligence work, but held besides a higher form of political use. In that period, such things as soothing the serving generals of the Northeast Army, and winning over the eminent men of Northeastern origin, may all be reckoned within the scope of political use. This, without a fair social standing and a powerful political background, one naturally could not do well.
Writing to this point draws out yet another matter of later date—one that may be called a consequence of the political use just spoken of. I take the chance to mention it here.

In 1934 Mr. Zhang Xueliang returned from a tour of study in Europe and took the post of deputy commander-in-chief of the Bandit-Suppression Headquarters for the three provinces of Henan, Hubei, and Anhui, quartered at Hankou. Perhaps having caught in Europe some political current, he seemed to have changed a little in thought, and so proposed to the concurrent commander-in-chief, Chairman Chiang, that the secret political organization already existing in the Northeast and Beiping—the "Society to Protect the East"—be dissolved; and asked that Commander-in-Chief Chiang appoint cadres to join with the cadres of the former "Society to Protect the East," after its dissolution, in forming together a new political body.

Mr. Zhang Xueliang's idea was to form a political organization inclined toward "Fascism"; Chairman Chiang consented only to appoint cadres to form a body upholding the Chinese tradition—propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame—and named it the "Siwei Society." Thus, plainly, the original "Fascist" flavor and its evident dictatorial leaning were corrected.

Those appointed to join the "Siwei Society," on the central side, were all cadres of the "Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People," among them Liu Jianqun, Deng Wenyi, Dai Li, Zheng Jiemin, Gan Guoxun, Ding Bingquan, Zhao Longwen, Qiu Kaiji, Han Wenhuan, and others. Save for Liu Jianqun alone, all were academy classmates. On the Northeastern side there were military and civil cadres both, among them Mao Zhuoran, Li Tiancai, Guan Jiyu, Yan Baohang, Gao Chongmin, Wang Yizhe, He Zhuguo, Liu Duoquan, and others. Whether the "Lixingshe" organization had by then been disclosed to the "Siwei Society" is not known; by my judgment, it was very likely kept secret.
Mr. Dai's position in the "Siwei Society" was quite important; one may say too that the forming of the "Siwei Society" was a fruit of his political use.

The "Siwei Society's" seat was at Hankou; Mr. Dai had many other tasks and could not attend to it as well, so he appointed Qiu Kaiji, the Special Services Department's man in charge at Hankou, to take part in its affairs regularly.

The Li Tiancai and Guan Jiyu spoken of before had old ties with Mr. Dai Yunong, and had had dealings with him in intelligence work besides, so that Mr. Dai's relations with Li Tiancai and Guan Jiyu were quite delicate. My meaning is that they may have leaned rather more toward Dai Yunong.

Because the "Siwei Society" was a "composite" political organization, lacking, in faith and in thought alike, the spirit of being "of one heart and one virtue," it ceased activity not long after its forming. Or, one may say, because a minority among the "Siwei Society" who had belonged to Zhang Xueliang's cadres were too dishonest, and had designs of egging Zhang Xueliang on to this and that, it was for that reason dissolved. Whether so or not, I cannot tell. As for whether the breaking-up of the "Siwei Society" had any bearing on the later "Xi'an Incident"—that is very hard to say, and here too I will not presume to guess.

To speak again of Mr. Dai's time at Beiping: his range of contact was very broad, and he gathered in no few excellent men, first and last. These men did not all necessarily join in the intelligence work proper; in his far-seeing view, they were mostly a store of talent kept for use. In the ten years and more that followed, that the work Mr. Dai led could develop in many directions beyond the bounds of secret-service work had, of course, much to do with this strong point of his—knowing men and using them well.

When he was fairly free, he did not rest either, but liked much to gather a few of us—Wang Tianmu, Wu Youquan, Mao Wanli, Wang Yunsun (secretary of the "Beiping Station," called the "Beiping know-it-all"), and the writer—and go out for a walk, most often to Beihai Park and Zhongshan Park. Sometimes too we would sit down at the Five-Dragon Pavilion in Beihai or the Laijinyuxuan in Zhongshan Park and drink a pot of tea, and now and then go to some small eating-house each of a distinct flavor. This was no idle pastime; to him it was a part of the work too—to observe a man, to understand a man, one can see more truly only in the small and trifling details.

Brother Mao Wanli, who came with Mr. Dai, had duties much like an ordinary confidential secretary's, though at that time there was as yet no formal title. When Mr. Dai had other activity, he too often lingered together with the writer; we had many points of temper in common, and, being besides free of ceremony, imperceptibly became fast friends. Our friendship was very pure, and may be called a natural growth, without a trace even of any thought of "convenience to the work." From then we have been friends fifty years, and are good friends still. People call us wine-and-meat friends; I hold that in making friends what harm is there in "wine and meat"—but there must be a bond of true hearts as well.
The friendship of brother Wanli and me, a bosom bond past our working rule, will be set down many times in the perilous life to come.

Mr. Dai was about to leave Beiping for the capital; before setting out, accompanied by Mr. Zheng Jiemin, he called on acting Chairman He, and went severally to the garrison front to pay respects to Huang Jie, commander of the Second Division, and Guan Linzheng, commander of the Twenty-Fifth Division. I think this was not merely a courtesy call or a leave-taking. What lay behind it, I had best not guess wildly.
The day before he left Beiping, Mr. Dai gathered the Beiping and Tianjin comrades for a talk at his lodging at Qifenglou—in fact, to listen to him speak.

The time appointed was ten in the morning; present were Zheng Jiemin, Xing Shan, Mao Wanli, Wang Tianmu, Yang Ying, Qi Nanpu, Bai Shiwei, Wang Yunsun, the writer, and others. Mr. Dai had done a little arranging in the parlor on the second floor of his lodging, just enough to hold ten men.

There was no ceremony at the time; before speaking, Mr. Dai was specially courteous with the Mr. Zheng Jiemin present, and then began to speak. He said a great deal, which, summed up, may be put in four points:
First, he analyzed the present situation, at home and abroad, and stressed the gravity of the North China situation.
Next, he directed that the "Beiping Station" and the "Tianjin Station" strengthen their working disposition—that is, open up intelligence lines on many sides.

Third, he set out the intelligence needs of the higher command: not only to gather every kind of concrete intelligence bearing on Japan's military moves and its support of traitors' work of sabotage, but to note especially the Communist Party's political intrigues and its intent to fish in troubled waters.
Last, he asked that each of us spur and school himself, enrich himself, and strengthen his working ability, that he might bear the heavy burden.
Mr. Dai, having finished speaking, again very respectfully asked "Mr. Jiemin" to give some views. Mr. Zheng, unable well to decline, drew out a few points along the lines Mr. Dai had spoken.

Mr. Dai asked Wang Tianmu and the writer too; brother Tianmu said nothing, and I had all the less to say. The speaking done, all were silent, nor did we exchange any views among ourselves. This too is where we differ from the common run. Then we took a plain meal there at Mr. Dai's, which was as good as a farewell dinner.

Mr. Dai went by train; in those days there was no aircraft from Beiping to Nanjing, and the handiest conveyance was the "Blue Steel express," the special fast train of the Tianjin–Pukou Railway. This "Blue Steel express," so called, had its body painted blue in outward form; in quality it was rather more solid; and its running was fast, punctual, and smooth—that was all. When we went to the station to see him off, I said a special "keep well" to brother Mao Wanli—truly a clasping of hands at parting, past bearing to let go. Mr. Dai knew too that we were fond of each other, and said: "I hope you two will cooperate well in the work."

A moment before the train started, Mr. Dai suddenly recalled a matter and charged me to see to it; I thought it something specially urgent, and raised my attention to hear his order, when he said: "That car I bought for someone—please keep it for the time being; it will be shipped off before long. On no account drive it about for fun—if it is damaged there will be trouble." So that was it; hearing it, I truly felt out of sorts.

It was a 1931 "Buick," eight cylinders, open-topped, bought secondhand to begin with, but well kept and still eight parts new; used for a spin, it would of course be very smart. This was a small matter, not worth a line here; but there just are such coincidences under heaven, and who would have thought that, in the near future, this car would win the first merit in our work.

On 4 May 1933, Mr. Zheng Jiemin, "special commissioner of the Juntong at Beiping," relayed through the night the urgent sanction order handed down by the highest military and political authorities in Beiping, setting a term of one week to report back.

Three days later, that is on 7 May of the same year, the "Beiping Station" and the "Tianjin Station" belonging to the "Juntong," working in concert, put to death Zhang Jingyao—that former military governor of Hunan, that leftover creature of a spent warlord, blinded by greed and lost to all national feeling, who was willing to be a claw and fang of the Japanese invaders—in the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lits in the "Legation Quarter" of Beiping, a special district where our government held no extraterritorial jurisdiction.

This forceful blow not only quelled the frenzied schemer's design to stir up disorder, but also shattered the plot drawn up by Itagaki Seishirō on behalf of the Japanese military. The influence of the case was such that it at once eased the extremely tense North China situation and steadied the frightened hearts of the Beiping and Tianjin people. Toward the preparations for a long war of resistance that could be calmly laid over the next four years, it worked a certain effect too.

It was learned afterward that the importance of this case far exceeded the common imagining; for Zhang Jingyao's treasonous activity in Beiping was of no single day, and, using every means of incitement, seduction, bribery, and deception in our highest military and political organs and in our fighting units, he had won over no few senior officials, among them even military commanders holding troops, and was on the point of launching a "mutiny" or a "coup." Had he not been cut off in good time, and a disaster dissolved before it took shape, the consequences would have been past bearing to contemplate.

The working unit at Beiping and Tianjin then, short of hands, crude in equipment, and having to report back within a set term on a matter come up all at once, yet did not fail its mission; we prided ourselves that it was a flawless and masterly stroke. And the man of the first merit in carrying through this case was Mr. Bai Shiwei, who is happily still living today.
